microscopy-001.question: In an infinity-corrected microscope, an objective is designed to give 40× when combined with a tube lens of focal length 200 mm. Which correctly pairs the focal length of this objective and the magnification it gives when mounted on another microscope whose tube lens has a focal length of 180 mm?
choices: Focal length 5 mm, and the magnification stays at the marked 40×
Focal length 5 mm, and the magnification becomes 36×
Focal length 5 mm, and the magnification becomes about 44×
microscopy-001.explanation: In an infinity-corrected system the object sits in the front focal plane of the objective, so the light leaving the objective is collimated, and the tube lens forms the image in its own focal plane. The lateral magnification is M = f_TL/f_obj, so f_obj = 200/40 = 5 mm. With a 180 mm tube lens, M = 180/5 = 36×. Keeping 40× is the mistake of thinking the magnification is set by the objective alone. About 44× inverts the ratio, giving 40 × 200/180 ≈ 44. Tube-lens focal lengths differ between manufacturers, so an objective from another maker gives a magnification different from its marking, and its aberration correction may not perform as designed.

microscopy-002.question: In Köhler illumination of a microscope, which element is located in a plane conjugate to the specimen plane (a plane imaged onto the specimen)?
choices: The field diaphragm
The condenser aperture diaphragm
The light source (the lamp filament)
microscopy-002.explanation: In Köhler illumination, the image of the light source is formed at the condenser aperture diaphragm (the condenser's front focal plane), and the condenser images the field diaphragm onto the specimen plane. The source is therefore not imaged onto the specimen, and the field is evenly lit even if the filament is uneven. Closing the field diaphragm only narrows the illuminated area, reducing stray light. The source and the aperture diaphragm are also conjugate to the back focal plane of the objective; this series sets the range of illumination angles, that is, the condenser's numerical aperture, and is not conjugate to the specimen. Imaging the source directly onto the specimen is called critical illumination, in which the source's unevenness overlaps the image.

microscopy-003.question: In a transmitted-light brightfield microscope, the condenser aperture diaphragm is closed down hard so that the illumination numerical aperture is much smaller than that of the objective. Which correctly describes the change in the image?
choices: The illumination angles become uniform and aberrations decrease, so the resolution also improves
Only the size of the illuminated field shrinks; resolution and contrast do not change
Contrast and depth of focus increase, but resolution drops and diffraction fringes become noticeable at the edges of objects
microscopy-003.explanation: The aperture diaphragm sets the range of illumination angles (the condenser's numerical aperture). In Abbe's theory of image formation, the more obliquely the illumination enters, the more easily light diffracted by fine structures in the specimen is captured by the objective, and the resolution limit is roughly λ/(NA_obj + NA_cond). Closing down to reduce NA_cond lowers the resolution, and as the illumination approaches coherence, diffraction fringes appear at edges, but contrast increases even for transparent specimens and the depth of focus grows. The option saying resolution improves has the direction reversed. Changing the illuminated area is the job of the field diaphragm, which is being confused with the aperture diaphragm. As a guide, the aperture diaphragm is set to about 70–80% of the objective's numerical aperture.

microscopy-004.question: A periodic grating-like specimen is observed with an objective of numerical aperture NA = 0.5, illuminated normally along the optical axis with collimated coherent light of wavelength 550 nm. In Abbe's theory, if the image of the grating forms when the zeroth order and a first diffraction order enter the objective, which is closest to the smallest period that can be imaged?
choices: About 1.1 µm
About 0.55 µm
About 0.67 µm
microscopy-004.explanation: When light strikes a grating of period d at normal incidence, the first diffracted order leaves in the direction sinθ = λ/d. The objective accepts angles with sinθ ≤ NA, so the condition for the first order to enter is d ≥ λ/NA = 0.55 µm/0.5 = 1.1 µm. With only the zeroth order the brightness is uniform and no grating fringes appear. About 0.55 µm is λ/(2NA), the limit when the illumination is tilted as far as possible so that the zeroth order and one first order enter at opposite edges of the aperture, which differs from the normal-incidence condition. About 0.67 µm is 0.61λ/NA, confusing this with the Rayleigh criterion for two incoherent points. The fineness of the image is set by the range of diffracted light that enters the objective.

microscopy-005.question: A fluorescence image at a wavelength of 520 nm is recorded with a camera through a 60×, numerical aperture 1.4 oil-immersion objective. Using the guideline that the specimen-plane resolution d = 0.61λ/NA should be sampled by at least 2 pixels (one pixel no larger than half of d at the camera plane), which is closest to the upper limit of the camera's pixel pitch? (Take the combined magnification of objective and tube lens as 60×.)
choices: About 13.6 µm
About 0.11 µm
About 6.8 µm
microscopy-005.explanation: The resolution at the specimen plane is d = 0.61 × 0.52 µm / 1.4 ≈ 0.227 µm. At the camera plane this is magnified 60 times to about 13.6 µm, so sampling it with at least 2 pixels requires a pixel pitch of 13.6/2 ≈ 6.8 µm or less. About 13.6 µm receives the resolution element with a single pixel, which samples too coarsely and buries detail in the pixels. About 0.11 µm forgets the magnification and compares sizes at the specimen plane. Making pixels needlessly small reduces the light per pixel and makes noise more prominent, so it is important to match the magnification to the pixel size. Taking the cutoff frequency 2NA/λ as the reference instead calls for even finer pixels of about 5.6 µm.

microscopy-006.question: In a transmitted-light darkfield microscope, the background is dark and tiny particles and thin structures appear to glow. Which correctly describes how this works?
choices: The illumination is linearly polarized with a polarizer, and a crossed analyzer removes the background light so that only birefringent structures appear bright

The illumination strikes the specimen only at angles larger than the objective's numerical aperture, so the direct illumination does not enter the objective and the image is formed only by light scattered or diffracted by the specimen
The phase of the illumination passing straight through the specimen is shifted by λ/4 so that it interferes constructively with the light diffracted by the specimen
microscopy-006.explanation: Darkfield illumination uses an annular stop that blocks the center of the condenser, or a dedicated condenser, so that the illumination strikes the specimen at angles larger than the objective's numerical aperture. The direct illumination passes by without entering the objective, so the background is dark, and only light scattered or diffracted by the specimen enters the objective to form the image. Even particles smaller than the resolution can therefore be detected as glowing points if they scatter enough light (their size is not rendered correctly). Because the illumination numerical aperture must exceed that of the objective, with high-NA objectives a type with a built-in iris diaphragm is used to reduce the numerical aperture. Viewing birefringence between crossed polarizers is how a polarizing microscope works, and shifting the phase of the direct light to make it interfere is how a phase-contrast microscope works.

microscopy-007.question: Colorless, transparent cells are observed with a phase-contrast microscope. Which correctly describes how contrast arises in the image?
choices: A sensitive camera amplifies the slight differences in how much light the cells absorb and turns them into brightness
The direction of the light changes with the refractive-index differences of the cell, and the amount by which the image position shifts is displayed as brightness

A phase plate in the back focal plane of the objective shifts the phase of the direct light that passed straight through the specimen by about λ/4, turning its phase relationship with the light diffracted by the specimen into differences in brightness
microscopy-007.explanation: A transparent specimen hardly changes the amplitude of light; it is a phase object that only delays the phase. When the phase delay φ is small, the transmitted light can be written exp(iφ) ≈ 1 + iφ, the sum of strong direct light and weak diffracted light shifted in phase by about π/2, and as it stands the intensity barely changes. In Zernike's phase-contrast method, a phase plate is placed where the direct light passing through the condenser's annulus gathers as a ring in the objective's back focal plane, shifting the phase of the direct light by about λ/4 and attenuating it. The direct and diffracted light then reinforce or cancel, and differences in phase become differences in brightness. For a specimen with almost no absorption, amplifying absorption differences shows nothing. The brightness comes from interference, not from shifts in image position, and bright halos at edges are characteristic of this method.

microscopy-008.question: When cells in a plastic culture dish are observed with a Nomarski-type differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope, the image contrast is often badly degraded. Which is the main reason?
choices: DIC uses two mutually orthogonal polarizations, so the plastic dish bottom, which is birefringent because of stress from molding, disturbs the polarization state and breaks the interference condition
Plastic strongly absorbs visible light, so the illumination used for DIC does not reach the specimen
Plastic has a lower refractive index than glass, so the numerical aperture of the objective drops and the resolution falls
microscopy-008.explanation: In DIC, linearly polarized light from a polarizer is split by a Nomarski prism into two beams of orthogonal polarization, shifted slightly sideways, and after passing through the specimen they are recombined and made to interfere at an analyzer. The difference in optical path between the positions the two beams pass, that is, the phase gradient, becomes brightness, giving a shaded, three-dimensional-looking image. This mechanism assumes the polarization states of the two beams are well defined, so passing through a plastic dish that is birefringent from injection-molding strain disturbs the polarization and the contrast is lost. A glass-bottom dish is therefore used, or phase contrast, which does not use polarization, is chosen instead. Culture-dish plastic absorbs almost no visible light, and the dish material does not lower the objective's numerical aperture either.

microscopy-009.question: A green fluorescent dye (absorption peak about 490 nm, emission peak about 520 nm) is observed with an epi-fluorescence microscope. Which combination of filter set is correct?
choices: The excitation filter passes about 510–550 nm, the dichroic mirror reflects light longer than about 500 nm, and the emission filter passes about 470–490 nm
The excitation filter passes about 470–490 nm, the dichroic mirror reflects light shorter than about 500 nm and transmits longer light, and the emission filter passes about 510–550 nm
The excitation and emission filters have the same band (about 480–530 nm), and a half mirror that splits the light equally is used instead of a dichroic mirror
microscopy-009.explanation: Fluorescence is emitted after the excited molecule loses part of its energy through vibrational relaxation, so it comes out at longer wavelengths than the excitation light (the Stokes shift). The excitation filter therefore selects only the short side of the absorption band (about 470–490 nm), the dichroic mirror reflects the excitation light toward the specimen and transmits the longer-wavelength fluorescence from the specimen, and finally the emission filter removes leaked excitation light and passes only about 510–550 nm to the detector. Fluorescence is often orders of magnitude weaker than the excitation light, and even slight leakage of excitation light buries it in background, so configurations with overlapping bands or a half mirror that loses half of the light each way are not used. In the combination with the wavelengths reversed, the dye is excited at longer wavelengths where it absorbs little, and almost no fluorescence is emitted at wavelengths shorter than the excitation, so almost nothing is seen.

microscopy-010.question: In a laser-scanning confocal microscope, which correctly describes the role of the pinhole placed in front of the detector?
choices: It raises the intensity of the excitation light so that no fluorescence is emitted outside the focal plane
It diffracts the laser light to widen the illuminated area so that the whole field of view is lit at once
Placed in a plane conjugate to the focal plane in the specimen, it blocks light coming from outside the focal plane, giving an image of only a thin layer along the optical axis (an optical section)
microscopy-010.explanation: In a confocal microscope, the objective focuses laser light to a single point in the specimen, and the fluorescence emitted there is collected by the same objective and detected through a pinhole at a position conjugate to the focus. Light from the focal plane is focused onto the pinhole and passes, but light from above or below the focal plane is spread out at the pinhole and is mostly blocked. This yields images of only a thin layer with little blur even in thick specimens, and stacking them while changing the focus gives a three-dimensional image. Fluorescence is still emitted outside the focus; the confocal approach removes it on the detection side, whereas not emitting fluorescence outside the focus is the mechanism of two-photon excitation. The image is built up pixel by pixel by scanning a point, so the whole field is not lit at once.

microscopy-011.question: In a confocal microscope using a 63×, numerical aperture 1.4 objective, the pinhole diameter is to be matched to the diameter of the Airy disk of the fluorescence (wavelength 520 nm) — the diameter of the first dark ring, 1.22λ/NA at the specimen plane (1 Airy unit). Taking the magnification at the pinhole plane as 63×, which is closest to the pinhole diameter?
choices: About 14.3 µm
About 28.5 µm
About 0.45 µm
microscopy-011.explanation: The Airy disk diameter at the specimen plane is 1.22λ/NA = 1.22 × 0.52 µm / 1.4 ≈ 0.453 µm. At the pinhole plane it is magnified 63 times, giving 0.453 × 63 ≈ 28.5 µm. About 14.3 µm uses the radius of the first dark ring, 0.61λ/NA, which is half the diameter. About 0.45 µm is the size at the specimen plane, forgetting the magnification. Making the pinhole smaller than 1 Airy unit makes the optical section slightly thinner, but the light passing through drops sharply and the signal-to-noise ratio falls. Making it larger brightens the image but lets out-of-focus light in, so about 1 Airy unit is commonly used. The longer the fluorescence wavelength, the larger the suitable pinhole.

microscopy-012.question: In a microscope, which correctly explains why the resolution along the optical axis (in depth) is worse (a larger value) than the lateral resolution?
choices: The objective collects light only over a limited range of angles from one side of the specimen, so the range of spatial frequencies it can capture is narrower along the optical axis than laterally
The axial resolution is set by the wavelength alone and does not change when the numerical aperture is increased
The lateral resolution is proportional to 1/NA and the axial to 1/NA², so with oil-immersion objectives whose NA exceeds 1 the axial resolution becomes the better of the two
microscopy-012.explanation: The spread of the point image is set by the range of angles the objective collects. Laterally, light at opposite edges of the aperture carries spatial frequencies up to 2n sinθ/λ, but along the axis there is only about n(1 − cosθ)/λ, so in a microscope collecting light from one side only, the axial bandwidth is narrower. As a guide, the lateral resolution is 0.61λ/NA and the axial 2nλ/NA²; with λ = 520 nm, NA = 1.4 and n = 1.518 these are about 0.23 µm and about 0.81 µm, so the axial resolution is more than 3 times worse. The axial resolution is inversely proportional to NA², so increasing NA has an even larger effect on it, and it is not set by the wavelength alone. The formula contains the refractive index n, and NA never exceeds n, so even with NA above 1 the axial resolution never surpasses the lateral.

microscopy-013.question: In total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy, excitation light of wavelength 488 nm strikes the interface between a coverslip (refractive index 1.518) and an aqueous solution (refractive index 1.33) at an angle of incidence of 70° and is totally reflected. Which is closest to the depth at which the intensity of the evanescent wave penetrating into the water falls to 1/e, d = λ/(4π√(n₁²sin²θ − n₂²))?
choices: About 75 nm
About 150 nm
About 950 nm
microscopy-013.explanation: n₁ sinθ = 1.518 × sin70° ≈ 1.426, so n₁²sin²θ − n₂² ≈ 2.035 − 1.769 = 0.266, whose square root is about 0.516. Then d = 488 nm / (4π × 0.516) ≈ 75 nm. About 150 nm uses 2π instead of 4π; it is the depth at which the field amplitude falls to 1/e, and for intensity the depth is half of that. About 950 nm forgets to divide by 4π. The excitation light reaches only about 100 nm from the interface, so only molecules near the cell membrane are observed, with little background. In the scheme where total reflection is produced through the objective, the objective's numerical aperture must be at least n₁ sinθ (about 1.43 in this example), so oil-immersion objectives with a numerical aperture of about 1.45–1.49 are used.

microscopy-014.question: Which correctly pairs the reason a two-photon excitation fluorescence microscope can obtain optical sections without a pinhole like that of a confocal microscope, and the excitation wavelength for two-photon excitation of a dye that is excited at 480 nm with one photon?
choices: The probability of absorbing two photons simultaneously is proportional to the square of the intensity, so excitation occurs only near the high-intensity focus. Excitation light of about 240 nm is used
Near-infrared light is not scattered in living tissue, so it does not reach anywhere other than the focus. Excitation light of about 960 nm is used

The probability of absorbing two photons simultaneously is proportional to the square of the intensity, so excitation occurs only near the high-intensity focus. Excitation light of about 960 nm is used
microscopy-014.explanation: In two-photon excitation, a molecule absorbs two photons almost simultaneously and is excited by the sum of their energies. The energy corresponding to 480 nm for one photon is shared between two photons, so each photon carries half the energy, that is, about twice the wavelength, 960 nm. About 240 nm is the mistake of halving the wavelength instead of adding the energies. The absorption probability is proportional to the square of the intensity, so strong excitation occurs only near the focus of focused femtosecond pulses, and almost no fluorescence is emitted outside the focus. No pinhole is therefore needed on the detection side, and even scattered fluorescence can be collected as signal. Near-infrared light scatters less than visible light and reaches deeper, but it is not free of scattering; the reason sections are obtained is the dependence on the square of the intensity.

microscopy-015.question: In a STED microscope, the area around the excited fluorescence spot is illuminated with an intense doughnut-shaped beam, and stimulated emission switches off the fluorescence there, narrowing the region that emits. Expressing the resolution as d ≈ d₀/√(1 + I/Is) (d₀ is the diffraction-limited resolution, I the STED beam intensity and Is the saturation intensity), which is closest to the resolution with d₀ = λ/(2NA), fluorescence wavelength λ = 600 nm, NA = 1.4 and I/Is = 15?
choices: About 13 nm
About 54 nm
About 214 nm
microscopy-015.explanation: d₀ = 600 nm/(2 × 1.4) ≈ 214 nm, and √(1 + 15) = 4, so d ≈ 214/4 ≈ 54 nm. About 13 nm is the mistake of dividing by 1 + I/Is = 16 without taking the square root. About 214 nm assumes that no method can beat the diffraction limit. In STED, the intensity at the center of the doughnut is zero, so fluorescence remains there, while around it stimulated emission returns molecules to the ground state so they do not emit. The stronger the STED beam, the closer the switched-off region creeps toward the center, and the emitting region becomes narrower than the diffraction limit. The focusing of light itself remains diffraction-limited; the idea of the method is to beat the limit by switching fluorescent molecules on and off nonlinearly. Photobleaching and damage from the intense STED beam are practical constraints.
